title: The genetic technique that finds (almost) every infection
content:
It identified Covid-19. Now this genetic technique is helping doctors to make life-or-death decisions.
In late December 2019, a team of virologists from three major Chinese cities began analysing swabs taken from patients hospitalised with mysterious cases of severe pneumonia.
All had been present at the Huanan Seafood Market, Wuhan, before rapidly falling unwell. But when the virologists ran the samples, they drew a blank: the genetic material did not match any previously discovered pathogen.
The doctors turned to a new screening method known as metagenomic testing. Instead of checking for known microbes, the test could reveal all the microorganisms present in the samples – previously identified or not.
It enabled them to see that the pathogen in the patients' samples bore a close resemblance to the coronavirus family, a group that included viruses which had previously caused outbreaks of severe pneumonia in humans, such as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (Mers). The scientists had just discovered Covid-19.
"It was a gamechanger compared with previous pandemics," says Niranjan Nagarajan, an associate professor at the National University of Singapore. Knowing what the pathogen was made it possible to rapidly develop Covid diagnostics to try to curb the spread, and kickstarted the frantic search for treatments and vaccines around the globe .
This remains the best-known use of metagenomics to date. But the test is now increasingly being used in hospitals. And from quickly diagnosing sepsis to identifying the causes of unexplained ailments, it's already saving lives.
Whenever a patient arrives in a neurological ward displaying signs of confusion and drowsiness, and complaining of fever, headache and weakness, doctors are acutely aware that it could be a life-or-death emergency.
How metagenomic testing works
Metagenomics, the study of all the DNA and RNA found in a particular environment, is seen as an increasingly important clinical approach . Metagenomic testing involves extracting genetic material from a sample, then using advanced sequencing methods to identify the genetic codes of everything that's there. These results can be analysed by computers with reference to large databases, allowing doctors to pinpoint the exact organisms present, such as bacteria or viruses.
This constellation of symptoms can indicate meningitis or encephalitis – deadly conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord. Yet doctors often face a critical dilemma. The most suitable treatment would depend on whether the patient's condition was due to a virus or bacteria, or an overreaction from the brain's immune system. With limited tests and time, however, doctors are often forced to hedge their bets.
"You need to make a decision immediately," says Charles Chiu, a professor and infectious diseases expert at the University of California San Francisco Department of Medicine in the US, who has been carrying out new studies into the use of metagenomic tests. "Currently, with patients who are critically ill, doctors treat them for infection and for autoimmune disease."
In some ways, this is contradictory, because it involves suppressing the patient's immune system even though they might have an infection. "But there's often no other choice," says Chiu.
Metagenomics is now helping to inform these decisions. Chiu and his colleagues have developed a pioneering metagenomics test for identifying pathogens within cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid that bathes the brain and spinal cord. The test has already flagged cases where, unbeknownst to doctors, a pathogen was driving a patient's symptoms.
For example, Chiu encountered a patient who had been diagnosed with meningitis and liver failure, and was scheduled to receive a liver transplant. But the metagenomics test on her spinal fluid revealed that she was actually infected with the hepatitis E virus. While hepatitis E is a known and treatable cause of liver disease, it is not commonly tested for in high-income countries such as the US.
"We gave her an antiviral medication, she got better, and we spared her from undergoing the transplant," says Chiu.
Until recently, the use of metagenomics has been limited by the length of time required for the analysis. Separating human and microbial DNA, and identifying the signs of a potentially worrisome pathogen, requires highly specialist skills. "Doing the sequencing and the analysis can take several days to a week," says Nagarajan. "The patient might die before you're able to get a result."
Now, though, machines can sequence DNA within as little as one to two hours, and AI tools can ingest vast datasets to decipher patterns within them. And it's finally making metagenomics more widely accessible.
For people with poorly functioning immune systems, any infection can swiftly turn into a potentially deadly threat. Transplant recipients, cancer patients undergoing immune-suppressing treatment and those living with autoimmune diseases must be on constant high alert.
Studies have suggested that immunosuppressed patients who develop sepsis or blood poisoning due to an infection are at a 23% higher risk of dying in hospital. However, making a quick diagnosis in these cases is not always easy.
ranking_reason: The article reports the discovery of a genetic technique that finds almost every infection, which has the potential to revolutionize disease diagnosis and treatment.

content: A giant elephant’s tooth has preserved clues to the watery world that sustained early humans nearly 700,000 years ago. Researchers studying elephant remains from Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (GBY-NBA) in northern Israel have reconstructed a Pleistocene environment rich in water, vegetation, and wildlife. Published in Quaternary Science Reviews , the study reveals the landscape shared by enormous mammals and some of the region’s earliest human toolmakers. Led by Hannah Farrell (a PhD candidate at Haifa University), the research examined molar and tusk fragments excavated by Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University of Kiryat Shmona in the Galilee and his colleagues. The site, Gesher Benot Ya’aqov (Daughters of Jacob Bridge), sits in the Jordan Rift Valley, south of today’s Hula Valley. The fossils belonged to Palaeoloxodon antiquus , the straight-tusked elephant, one of the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene. Nearby basalt handaxes and cleavers place early humans in the same setting. These tools belong to the Acheulian tradition, among the earliest and most geographically widespread stone tool technologies in human history. The tooth offered more than a way to identify the animal. Its structure, microscopic wear, and chemical composition provided different lines of evidence about its life and surroundings. The team combined CT scanning, 3D reconstruction, microscopic wear analysis, isotope geochemistry, and pollen studies to piece together the broader ecosystem. The results point to an enduring landscape of woodlands, grasslands, marshes, rivers, and shallow-water habitats. Carbon isotope values suggest that the elephant lived where water remained consistently available. Pollen recovered from sediments added detail to that picture, revealing reeds, sedges, willows, tamarisks, and aquatic plants. Together, the findings suggest that the Hula Valley region was a stable ecological refuge within the Levantine Corridor, the land bridge connecting Africa and Eurasia. Reliable water and biological resources likely made this landscape a valuable stopping point or habitat for wildlife and human groups moving through the region. According to Sharon, “understanding how humans and animals responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps us better understand the forces that shaped our species.” “The availability of water, vegetation, and animal resources shaped where humans and wildlife could survive,” Sharon says. “The wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley helped sustain life along one of the world’s earliest migration corridors, offering a rare opportunity to understand the ecological conditions that supported both animals and human populations nearly 700,000 years ago.” Reference: “Elephant dental remains from the Acheulian site at North Bridge Acheulian–Gesher Benot Ya’aqov: hominin behavior and environmental implications” by Hannah Farrell, Gonen Sharon, Minji Jin, Dafna Langgut, Cheryl A. Makarewicz and Nimrod Marom, 14 September 2026, Quaternary Science Reviews . DOI: 10.1016/j.quascirev.2026.110277 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .
ranking_reason: Breakthrough discovery about the ecological conditions that supported early human populations nearly 700,000 years ago.

content: Once pushed to the brink, giant tortoises on a Seychelles atoll now outnumber the country’s people, with a new survey estimating nearly 183,000 animals. Aldabra Atoll, home to the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population, supports an estimated 180,000 animals, according to research led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter. The highest estimate yet for the Aldabra giant tortoise ( Aldabrachelys gigantea ) reflects both a remarkable conservation recovery and a better way of counting animals that are difficult to see. Published in Ecology and Evolution , the study analyzed monitoring records collected by SIF staff from 2018 through 2022. It delivers the first rigorous estimate covering the atoll and replaces the widely quoted figure of about 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s. The team’s best estimate was almost 183,000 adult and subadult tortoises, more than the entire human population of the Seychelles. Their numbers appeared relatively stable during the study period. That abundance would have been difficult to imagine in the 19th century, when heavy exploitation reduced Aldabra’s tortoises to fewer than 1,000. Their recovery has been supported by decades of protection, including the atoll’s designation as a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Today, Aldabra and the Galapagos are the two remaining strongholds of native wild giant tortoises, with far fewer animals in the Galapagos. The new findings strengthen Aldabra’s reputation as one of the Indian Ocean’s outstanding conservation successes. “The monitoring data in this study were collected by SIF staff living and working on the atoll, year after year. More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra,” said Dr. Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF. The larger total comes with an important qualification: it does not mean the population has nearly doubled since 1999. A tortoise can be present without being visible, and earlier surveys did not adequately account for animals concealed in scrub or shade. Those estimates probably missed a substantial number. To address that problem, the researchers used Bayesian hierarchical distance sampling. This statistical method accounts for animals that observers failed to detect and for differences in visibility across habitats. It produces an estimate of the population, rather than simply a tally of sightings. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest-running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said study co-author Dr. Nancy Bunbury. “By modeling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.” The animals were most concentrated in Aldabra’s grasslands, known as “tortoise turf.” The next highest densities occurred on open exposed surfaces and in open mixed scrub. Dense scrub, mangroves, and Pemphis vegetation made tortoises harder to detect. Correcting for those differences helps researchers distinguish places with fewer animals from places where animals are simply harder to spot. Together, the findings describe a population that has recovered dramatically from historical exploitation and now appears healthy and stable. They also establish a more dependable starting point for measuring future changes, something direct comparisons with older estimates cannot provide. Despite their recovery, Aldabra’s tortoises face growing environmental pressures. Droughts are projected to become longer and more frequent, reducing food and shade, while rising seas threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitats. Feral goats, which devastated Aldabra’s vegetation, were eradicated in 2012. But feral cats and black rats remain and prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The researchers say planned efforts to eliminate these mammals could allow more young tortoises to survive, support further population growth, and help the species withstand climate pressures. “These results are great news for the tortoises and a testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr. Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter in Cornwall who helped develop the statistical framework used to analyze the monitoring data. “But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline, not an endpoint. Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought, and invasive species.” Reference: “Inferring the Abundance of an Island Megaherbivore From Semi-Structured Distance Sampling” by Lara B. Hillyard, Nancy Bunbury, Christopher N. Kaiser-Bunbury, Dave Hodgson, Luke A’Bear, Cheryl L. Sanchez, Christopher W. Jones, April Burt, Frauke Fleischer-Dogley and Dave W. Hudson, 4 September 2026, Ecology and Evolution . DOI: 10.1002/ece3.74282 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .
ranking_reason: The discovery of nearly 183,000 giant tortoises on Aldabra Atoll reflects remarkable conservation recovery and provides a benchmark for tracking the population in the future.

analysis.reason: The discovery of nearly 183,000 giant tortoises on Aldabra Atoll reflects remarkable conservation recovery and provides a benchmark for tracking the population in the future.
